Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): okay everyone hi, i'm Jordan from Redwood Inference, thanks for carving out the time. um we were planning a quick ~30 to 45 minute runthrough of our hosted chat API, then a quick tour of the console and Optimize suggestions, and leave time for Q&A. sound good?
[00:23] Emily (Aurora CTO): yeah that works, thanks. quick ask from our side — we want to understand streaming behavior because our UI shows partial replies as they arrive. we also care a lot about latency and per-token costs.
[00:38] Priya (Redwood SE): great, we'll demo streaming first. note that in hosted mode streaming is server-sent-events style chunks, you get fragments of tokens. the SDKs handle reassembly but if you do a custom websocket client you might see fiddly boundaries, uh sometimes punctuation attaches to previous chunk, so you should buffer a small window for UI smoothing.
[01:05] Marcus (Lead Eng): quick question — if a stream fails mid-response what's the recommended retry behavior? we don't want duplicate visible content to users.
[01:14] Priya: good one. two patterns: 1) idempotency + client side dedupe — we use a client-provided idempotency key per user-turn, server can resume or return an error; 2) use conservative retries with heuristics — e.g., only retry if fewer than N tokens emitted or if the error code is retryable. for streaming we recommend a short backoff and then resume from last confirmed token if you maintain server-side prefixes via our prefix caching API.
[01:45] Nikhil (Security): when you say prefix caching, is that stored on Redwood infrastructure or can it sit in our VPC/private deployment?
[01:53] Leo (Product): both. hosted customers get prefix cache on our infra with retention controls, and for Private/VPC deployments the cache stays customer-side. for hosted we offer opt-in controls for TTL and encryption-at-rest.
[02:10] Jordan: i'll also flag that Console -> Optimize will highlight cacheable prompt patterns and recommend which prompts to pin for caching.
[02:22] Sofia (Platform): can you briefly show the console where that recommendation appears?
[02:28] Jordan: sure — switching screens. (screen share noises) in Console, under Optimize -> Recommendations, you'll see 'high hit-rate prefixes' and 'batching opportunities' with estimated cost savings. 
[02:45] Priya: back on streaming specifics — streaming packets include a cursor position. clients should checkpoint after receiving a packet with a full token boundary. if a retry comes back with overlapping tokens, client logic should dedupe by cursor. also, for visible UX, show a typing indicator until final chunk is received.
[03:10] Marcus: ok. what's the rough p95 latency for short prompts (<= 64 tokens) on hosted?
[03:17] Priya: depends on model and selected slot, but for our verified models on hosted we see p95 between 110–220ms token-to-token for smaller autoregressive models. end-to-end first-byte for 64-token responses is often in the 250–600ms range. if you need <100ms p95 you might consider Dedicated in a nearby region or model selection with optimized kernels.
[03:45] Emily: and cost? how does aggressive batching trade off?
[03:49] Leo: batching reduces per-token cost but increases tail latency — Optimize will recommend batching windows tuned to your throughput. e.g., 50ms batching window can cut cost by ~15–30% for high-concurrency workloads but will add 30–70ms to p95 depending on traffic shape.
[04:10] Marcus: currencies — how do you bill streaming tokens? incremental or final?
[04:14] Jordan: billed per token emitted. streaming doesn't change billing model; you can see token breakdowns per-request in Console. we also have token caps and per-route quotas to prevent runaway costs.
[04:25] Nikhil: SOC2 — we need the cert and details on key management. also audit logs for model access.
[04:31] Jordan: yes, SOC2 is available. we support KMS integration and bring-your-own-key (BYOK) for Private. audit logs are available in Console with retention controls (30/90/365 days options as an add-on). i'll attach the SOC2 and a short KMS integration note after the call.
[04:58] Priya: quick demo of retry pseudo-code — (screen share) this is a small client flow: send request with idempotency key, stream tokens, checkpoint cursor, on retry check server side for resume token, if not available then reissue with prefix from cache. for web clients we show a sample that waits 100ms before rendering first chunk to avoid flicker.
[05:40] (brief cross talk)
[06:02] Emily: do you provide SDKs for node/python and mobile? our frontend team is on react native.
[06:08] Jordan: yes SDKs for JS, Python, and a lightweight mobile wrapper for React Native. note: mobile wrappers emphasize small buffer windows to save bandwidth.
[06:18] Marcus: ok about retries again — if a user gets a duplicate line because the client retried, how do you suggest masking that?
[06:25] Priya: dedupe by idempotency key + token cursor; for small duplication you can post-process at UI layer to collapse repeated prefixes. we also recommend server-side snippet hashing to detect duplicates.
[06:45] Sofia: let's speak about model params — temp, top_p, max_tokens. what are the defaults and which ones most customers tune?
[06:52] Leo: defaults are 0.8 temp, top_p 0.95, and max_tokens set per-route. customers typically lower temperature for deterministic behavior (0.0–0.3) for retrieval-augmented tasks and raise for creative tasks. Console has profile presets like 'deterministic', 'conversational', and 'creative'.
[07:18] Marcus: any guardrails on max_tokens? like safety or token limits?
[07:22] Priya: we enforce per-request token limits (model-dependent). you can also set route-level caps so a single user can't blow budget. plus safety filters run in the pipeline and can truncate or block outputs based on policy.
[07:38] Emily: show us an end-to-end example for chat where a user asks a long multi-turn question and we need stateful context.
[07:45] Priya: sure, demo time — we send a conversation history as prefix, use prefix cache for repeated system prompts, then call chat endpoint with streaming true. (demo plays out) note — you'll see in the console trace a breakdown: prompt tokens, KV cache hit %, and estimated per-request cost.
[08:30] Jordan: on the console trace — we have columns for 'model', 'latency', 'token count', and 'cache hit rate' so platform teams can trace expensive routes.
[08:45] Marcus: can we automate rollouts? e.g. split traffic between a higher-performance quantized model and a cheaper one?
[08:52] Leo: yes — Console -> Rollouts supports percentage-based splits and automatic fallback policies. you can do canary 10% to new model with auto-fallback to the older model on elevated error rates. there's also an experiment dashboard showing latency/cost/quality delta.
[09:22] Emily: quality delta — do you hook up evals against our prompt set?
[09:26] Priya: we can run a small eval harness in Redwood Optimize using your supplied prompt set; it'll score outputs and produce a regression alert if quality drops after model/quantization changes.
[09:40] Nikhil: for enterprise we need VPC or on-prem option; what's the onramp look like?
[09:46] Jordan: Private has a control plane and optional data plane inside your VPC. onboarding includes a connectivity window and a small managed install for on-prem kernels. typical lead time for Private is 8–12 weeks, Dedicated is 2–4 weeks depending on commitments.
[10:05] Marcus: latency for Private — are we looking at lower tail latencies?
[10:09] Priya: yes, because you can colocate and control instance sizing. Private also allows local KV caches which reduce cold-start costs.
[10:18] Sofia: can Optimize recommend quantization profiles? we run microservice inference with varying seq lengths.
[10:24] Leo: Optimize analyzes token distribution and suggests quantization and batching — it will say e.g., q4_0 for conversational short sequences vs q5_1 for longform. recommendations include estimated CPU/GPU perf and expected quality impact.
[10:40] Marcus: demo the Optimize panel?
[10:43] Jordan: (screen share) under Optimize -> Model Recommendations you can upload a sample trace and it'll produce a 'suggested profile' with expected savings and a quality delta. you can accept the recommendation and schedule a canary rollout.
[11:05] (Discussion continues with clarifying questions; timestamps jump forward as demo continues)
[21:12] Priya: here's a common failure mode — partial SSE stream followed by connection reset. server will usually emit an error code. recommended client pattern: on network error check whether server reported final token; if not then call replay endpoint with last cursor. if that's not available, fall back to a safe reissue with same idempotency key but with UI showing 're-synthesizing last reply' to avoid confusing users.
[25:03] Marcus: how do you surface retryable vs non-retryable errors in SDK?
[25:10] Priya: SDKs surface error classes: retryable (5xx, transient), non-retryable (4xx), and partial-stream. partial-stream errors include a 'cursor' param. we add helper utils that do resume automatically with a single backoff.
[29:57] Emily: for cost forecasting, can Console provide per-route burn rate and alerts?
[30:05] Jordan: yes, Console has per-route cost dashboards and alerting thresholds; you can tie them to Slack or PagerDuty for ops.
[32:40] Nikhil: audit log retention — can we export logs to our SIEM?
[32:45] Leo: yes S3 export or direct SIEM forwarding. logs include request id, model, route, token counts, and user-id hash (not PII).
[35:10] Sofia: we want to run a perf benchmark — what's typical data you need?
[35:16] Priya: a representative prompt set, concurrency profile, and desired SLO (e.g., p95 < 400ms). we'll run a benchmark on hosted with your sandbox key and return a report with latency/cost tradeoffs and Optimize suggestions.
[36:02] Marcus: timeline for that?
[36:05] Jordan: can do this week if you can share prompts — we'll try to run a quick run within 72 hours.
[36:12] Emily: ok we'll share a 200-row prompt CSV and expected concurrency numbers.
[36:18] (short discussion on account provisioning)
[38:40] (closing recap)
[38:55] Jordan: recap: i'll send SOC2 and KMS notes, we'll create a sandbox account for Aurora, Priya will prepare perf checklist and run with your prompts. Marcus to share prompt CSV. we'll schedule the perf call and a second deep-dive for security if needed.
[39:20] Emily: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[39:24] Jordan: any last questions?
[39:26] Marcus: none from me.
